newsitem.title: MEXICO: Left-wing Mexico City victor foresees progress.
newsitem.headline: Left-wing Mexico City victor foresees progress.

text.p: He has just three years to combat the urban nightmare of the largest city in the Americas, but leftist Mexico City mayoral winner Cuauhtemoc Cardenas is confident he will fulfil his electoral mandate.

"It will be the people who will have to judge whether or not the city has advanced as they expected," Cardenas told Reuters in an interview on Monday. "But I think the people are also sensible and know that some things come before others."

With ballots counted from 82.41 percent of the polling booths in Sunday's election, Cardenas, running for the Party of the Democratic Revolution (PRD), had won 47.78 percent of the vote. Alfredo del Mazo of President Ernesto Zedillo's Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) trailed with 25.55 percent, and Carlos Castillo Peraza of the right-wing National Action Party (PAN) took 15.92 percent.

For his interview, Cardenas wore a more sober tie than the bright yellow one with the party's colours that he had sported the night before at a triumphant rally of at least 25,000 supporters in the city centre.
And the usual dour look had returned to his features as he concentrated on his mayoral goals rather than his electoral triumph.
"I believe we can make a lot of progress in security, combating organised crime, fighting corruption and reducing administrative red tape," Cardenas said.
Also facing the new mayor will be such problems as smog levels that are among the world's highest, a grave water shortage, soaring rates of violent crime and a city deficit of almost $1.7 billion.

Cardenas has not flinched at the task before him, predicting there will be "significant advances" in his three-year term. He expressed confidence he would fulfil not only his election promises but also the hopes he instilled in a population eager for change from the long-ruling PRI.
To boost the economic recovery of Mexico's largest city, Cardenas proposed boosting public works projects, promoting tourism and cutting the red tape that discourages new business.
But he remained reticent about speculation that his real goal is the 2000 presidential election.
"Obviously the (PRD) party will look to win all the coming elections, independent of what personal decisions I make," Cardenas said.
The son of one of Mexico's best-loved presidents, Lazaro Cardenas, Cuauhtemoc Cardenas suffered defeats in the last two elections for Mexico's top post.
Many Mexicans believe he was cheated of victory in 1988 by fraud, but in 1994, after a lackluster campaign, he lost in an election generally regarded as clean.
"We have finally succeeded in having real elections in Mexico, elections in which the votes are what decides who governs and who represents the people," Cardenas said.
The relatively clean elections on Sunday dispelled most fears of fraud, or what Cardenas called "results fabricated in government offices."

Playing down fears of confrontation, Cardenas said he anticipated cooperation from the federal government, which still holds the reins on Mexico City's budget, its police force and the attorney general's office.
"I expect that we will establish a very tight and positive coordination," Cardenas said, noting the encouraging sign of Zedillo's late-night appearance on television to congratulate him.
